newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican peso strength seen hurting export stocks.
newsitem.headline: Mexican peso strength seen hurting export stocks.

text.p: The strength of the peso has begun taking a toll on export stocks on the Mexican Bolsa, putting off foreign investors and hastening their move into money market instruments, analysts said.
"There is a peso impact on the bolsa, there's a lack of interest, indeed there's caution among investors," Alonso Cervera, analyst at Mexican brokerage Interacciones, said.

The hardest hit sector has been export stocks, whose slide on the stock exchange has reflected a withering trade surplus recently, as a robust peso cuts into the competitive pricing of Mexican goods sold abroad.

Monclova-based steel maker and major exporter Ahmsa shares fell from 53.30 pesos on Sept. 20 to 48.50 pesos at the end of that month, a decline also seen in the share prices of exporters Alfa, Desc, Sanluis and Tamsa.

"If the peso is strong, things go badly for exporters," said Javier Maldonado, economist at Bancomer. "They sell the same amount of dollars for less pesos, which has obliged them to turn their focus on the domestic market."
The impact of an appreciating peso has shown up clearly in the latest trade surplus data for August. The surplus shrank to $264 million from $438 million in July.

According to Interacciones, exports grew at an annual rate of 10.1 percent in August, the lowest level since July 1993 and "significantly less than the average growth of 27.4 percent that was registered between 1995 and July 1996."
"What we need is not (peso) stability, but a more dynamic exchange rate," said Hector Velez, an analyst at Inverlat brokerage.

The exchange rate has held above the 1995 close of 7.70 pesos per dollar all this year despite inflation estimated at around 25-30 percent, which means in real terms it has gained in strength. The peso has moved in a range of 7.39 and 7.67.

Investors, many who are hearing analysts' predictions of a year-end exchange rate around 8 pesos per dollar, fear making an agressive assault into Mexican stocks, lest a sudden last quarter peso slide cuts through any potential capital gains.

Hence, analysts and traders say, you have a wait-and-see attitude from big money managers, while some speculators are making short-term forays into the market and getting out quickly with their peso profits intact.

Analysts say the reluctance toward the stock market is counter-balanced by strong investments in Mexico's Treasury, or Cetes, market, in what one analyst described as a flight-to-quality move because the market is showing less volatility.
In Tuesday's primary Cetes auction, demand was among the highest on record, at 17.44 billion pesos. Cetes rates continued to fall across the board.
The fall in interest rates, as well as a strong U.S. stock and Treasury market, helped spur a recovery in the stock market in the last two sessions after eight consecutive declines.
